lignes.texte: Most people think Roblox is a harmless digital playground for kids… it’s not.
But behind the scenes it’s something much more sinister. An unregulated,
addictive financial machine that was designed for endless growth.
No matter the cost.
But now, the long delayed reckoning is here.
For the first time, this empire built on amateur youth creators has collided with the law,
and the price of doing business on Roblox may be too high for much of its fanbase.
The entire might be changing forever and the game you know… is dead.
At first glance, Roblox seems to be the perfect mousetrap.
It’s a major gaming platform designed around letting users program their own games. Founders
David Baszucki and Eric Cassel developed a simple block based sandbox where players
code their own interactive worlds. The site became a massive ecosystem,
allowing millions to practice their coding skills, and build global communities.
And it succeeded beyond its creators’ wildest dreams.
Today, Roblox has a user-base of over 85 million daily users. Its top players have
monetized game design to the point of becoming literal millionaires.
But the most shocking aspect is the chokehold it has on American children.
Roughly half of kids under 16 are regular Roblox users.
While a small number design their own worlds, the majority play in other people’s sandboxes.
For this generation, Roblox is a rite of passage that serves as their first form of social media.
And that’s why the empire is collapsing.
Roblox operates on different levels: you can create games, play them,
customize avatar skins and build trophy cases. But the most controversial element
is its connections list. It’s similar to a friend list on Facebook or Twitter, where users can add
up to a thousand players, message each other in real time or voice-chat inside a shared
game experience. While many have met life-long friends on the site, it poses a huge question…
Is it actually safe?
Most major platforms, like Facebook, require users to be 13 years old. A
growing global push has demanded social media restrictions on kids. Australia even
banned all kids under 16 from social media, forcing millions off their existing accounts.
But Roblox slipped through the cracks.
The company argues it isn’t considered a social media site. By claiming it’s
primarily a gaming platform, it managed to bypass the bands.
And that gave Roblox its first black eye of many.
Today, around 40% of users on Roblox are under 13 years old. That makes
it the youngest-skewing major website, far bigger than kid-friendly gaming sites like
Neopets or Club Penguin. But those sites were heavily monitored and moderated. By comparison,
Roblox is the Wild West. For years, there were no age restrictions at
all. No one knew if they were playing with a 12-year-old or a 40-year-old.
In 2024, public anger boiled over.
Police reports revealed that at least 30 people had been arrested since 2018 for
targeting children on the site. The crisis became so severe, it led to vigilante “To
Catch a Predator” stings in the game. Facing a public relations nightmare, roblox made
changes. They banned users under 13 from social hangouts and blocked their direct messages.
But was it enough?
Millions of unsupervised players flood the site daily, intersecting directly with adult players.
While the site’s 2024 updates made it harder to contact them, communications between players are
still mostly unmonitored. Most of the time, users don’t know who is on the other side of the screen.
But as dangerous as the social features are, most players aren’t even looking at the chats.
They’re focused on something else entirely.
Roblox is more than a social media and gaming site. It’s a massive self-contained economy fueled
by its own currency… Robux. This digital money lets people create and buy virtual items to give
their account a unique flair. You can buy Robux individually, subscribe to a service called Roblox
Plus that offers bonuses, or earn Robux through games and contests. One of the biggest drivers
of the economy on Roblox is limited-time items, similar to NFTs, that become a rare status symbol
once they expire. That can lead to a rush to get the needed number of Robux before it’s too late.
And that’s another area where kids are vulnerable.
In recent years, Roblox has become overrun with scams. Most of them claim
to be offering free Robux, leading people to give information about their logins. Soon,
they find themselves locked out of accounts that took years to build. In the best-case scenario,
limited-time items get transferred to the scammer’s account. In worst-case scenarios,
the scammer can get ahold of credit card numbers that allow them to take
their theft into the real world. This was so common that Roblox had to add a feature
that allows players to “rollback” their account and get transferred items back.
But the scams in the game are nothing compared to the scam being run by the platform.
The richest people on the sitearen’t actually gamers. They’re developers who have turned
Roblox into a digital goldmine. They sell game passes, special features,
bonus levels and of course, skins and other limited-edition collectibles.
The top creators pull in millions of Robux. Some are billionaires in the virtual world.
But that doesn’t translate to real life.
The full-time designers wanted to monetize their creations and Roblox was more than happy
to help. The company introduced DevEx, a program where developers can exchange their hard-earned
Robux for real-world currency. But it came with massive strings attached. To qualify for a payout,
the Robux had to be earned strictly through in-site activity. Things like game passes,
custom collectibles or creator engagement milestones. Purchased Robux
or standard item reselling weren’t included. For a while, it seemed too good to be true.
Eventually, it was.
Currently, Roblox is making headlines for raising its rates from $.0035 per Robux to $.0038. But
that actually means that if someone has 30,000 Robux - the minimum to cash out - they’re
only going to earn $114. That’s the standard rate.
The company recently introduced a new rate for 18+ creators,
offering them $.0054 per Robux. This is seen as a way to entice older players
and creators and help the site get away from its reputation as a kids’ playground.
But will it be enough?
Roblox is a case of feast and famine. A select few people have become incredibly
wealthy by creating games that have become a money machine. The top earner on the site is rip_indra,
who created the addictive fighting game Blox Fruits, boasting a net worth of over
900 million Robux. If they cashed out today, they would be a millionaire.
But for the other 99%, it’s a struggle.
Currently, less than 1% of developers on the site make a living wage off the site.
The site is immensely competitive. Trying to stand out amid 40 million other games
is like finding a needle in a haystack. Most games simply get buried in volume,
and are lucky to get a small number of dedicated players who are willing to spend Robux on them.
That’s before the company takes its share.
The math is constantly working against creators before they even get out of the
gate. When a player buys a game pass or other developer product, Roblox immediately takes 30%
off the top as a marketplace fee. Add in the DevEx multiplier and Roblox’s developer cut
is more than double the standard take rate of major platforms like Apple, Google, and Steam.
The house always wins.
While the cash-out rate is fairly low for developers, the same can’t be said for the
cash-in rate. Many players, unable to earn enough Robux in-game to satisfy their addiction, resort
to buying Robux directly or through gift cards. Compared to the standard $.0038 exchange rate for
DevEx, the Robux purchase rate is much higher - coming in at $.0125, almost four times the rate of
what creators will get back out if they succeed. Between that and the high level needed for cashing
out, the majority of Roblox developers will never wind up seeing any real money from their games.
Is this even sustainable?
Roblox has built its entire economy on two pillars. On one end, there
are developers. Many of them are young, taking their first step into the world
of game development. This is their first chance to earn money for their creations,
and they don’t know if they’re being underpaid. Others are more experienced, and have spent years
grinding to build their collection and their reputation. Without this talent,
the sandbox won’t have the experiences needed to keep bringing in new players.
Because those new players are the core of Roblox’s success.
Roblox is the only major gaming website where such a huge percentage of its users are kids,
and they are the backbone of the site’s traffic. They don’t have
as much disposable income as adults, but they are a lot easier to hook. For years,
these kids were playing obsessively and scraping for every Robux they could earn in
order to pick up rare collectibles. Roblox built an unbeatable system. On one side,
underpaid developers. On the other, addicted kids who spend all their free time on the site.
And now, Uncle Sam is taking notice.
After the initial controversy over Roblox’s lax policies for younger players, the site
continued to add new safety features. But it was soon clear the band-aids it was offering
wouldn’t be sufficient to appease angry legislators. State authorities in Ohio,
Texas, Louisiana, Tennessee, Nebraska, and Oklahoma filed lawsuits against Roblox,
arguing that the company had failed on child safety and deceived parents. In
2026, the company announced it would require age verification for players.
That opened up a whole new can of worms.
On the surface, the new system seemed incredibly simple. People had to submit either a government
ID, or a selfie via Roblox’s system to verify their age. This was designed to
make sure no one was lying their way into 13+ games and communities. For most adult players,
it was very easy to get verified. But many kids, especially those below the age of 13 struggled.
Which meant it was time to face the camera.
At first, the system seemed foolproof. The camera’s algorithm analyzes facial features
and spits out an estimated age range. To prove its accuracy, the company even publicized a test
they did where a kid tried to fool the system with a fake moustache. And failed miserably.
The company followed this up by introducing more age-tiered accounts. Depending on the age group,
messages were blocked or limited. It seemed like Roblox was taking child safety seriously.
So why are so many people so angry?
2026 has been a disastrous year for the Roblox brand on the stock market, seeing consistent
slides and only minor peaks. It started the year at around $81 a share and peaked at 84 that
same month. Since then it’s lost almost half its value. And when it does drop, it’s usually steep.
One day in August 2026 saw a fall of 20%. That can’t be explained by market fluctuations.
Investors are losing faith in Roblox.
The biggest complaint people have with Roblox is that they don’t trust it to safeguard
their data. There’s an old expression, if something is being given away for free,
you’re the product. Roblox has always been free to play, but the goal was to get
players to spend money on Robux, gamepasses, and collectibles. Especially impulsive kids. But now,
the company has something else to give away. Hundreds of millions of people have uploaded
their personal data to the company’s servers. And that’s raised fears of potential data breaches.
For those who have scanned their IDs online, it’s a valid concern. A government ID may have enough
information to aid in identity theft, and there are millions of IDs in Roblox’s servers. Roblox
has tried to assuage users over this, saying that their servers are secure. While countless accounts
have been breached in hacks, the company itself has protected its databases. Still, the risk of a
hack has made many people drift towards the selfie option as the simplest way to verify their age.
Even that comes with risks.
Pictures are fed into a complex AI algorithm that extracts biometric data,
cross-referencing the user’s face against a massive database to estimate their
age. Currently, there are over 338 million images in the Roblox server.
Which means users don’t just take a selfie.
They’re handing over their biometrics to a corporate giant.
And with the explosion of AI software, how much of it is actually secure?
Could a harmless selfie sent to a gaming platform end up in a government database?
While Roblox claims to delete the data instantly, the growing panic has left people
demanding answers. Why would a company enforce a feature no one really wanted in the first place?
They didn’t have a choice.
The government has been breathing down Roblox’s neck for a while,
but 2026 was when it became too intense to ignore. A complaint was filed with the US
Federal Trade Commission in May 2026, calling for an investigation into unfair and deceptive
practices that endanger children and make them vulnerable to exploitation. The company
immediately denied the allegations and the FTC hadn’t issued a finding against Roblox. But
the suit was enough to scare investors, leading to another menacing stock drop.
And this has been coming for a long time.
According to Roblox’s financial disclosures, in the first quarter of 2026, the company set aside
$57 million in expenses for legal settlements with individual states. The exact details aren’t known,
as all were settled out of court and didn’t involve any legal findings against the company.
But what it indicates is that the company is running scared.These lawsuits as a legitimate
threat and if it doesn’t act quickly, its whole business model might be in danger.
Now Roblox is panicking.
As of 2026, the company has cut its full-year projections by up to $1 billion,
forecasting grim financial news that will no doubt lead to more stock losses. This
is due to a number of factors, but the age verification will be the biggest part. Users
will be forced off the site due to being unable to verify. A large percentage will
be children who find their accounts restricted and lose interest in the
platform. Others won’t want to hand over their data to Roblox. When these projections hit,
the company took another nasty stock drop, losing up to 22% of its value in extended trading.
But was this a surprise… or an inevitability?
For a long time, Roblox was one of the most unique business models in the tech
world. It built a massive online economy based around an audience that doesn’t have its own
money to spend. It took some of the most disliked elements of video gaming, like microtransactions,
and made them so addictive that it became the premier pastime among school children. And it
did this all without developing its own products beyond the initial operating systems. Instead,
it let millions of players design their own experiences and give the platform a hefty cut.
And now it’s catching up with them.
Roblox’s virtual economy might have earned billions, but behind the scenes, it was based
on exploitation. Developers were paid pennies on the dollar. Meanwhile, the kids who were playing
obsessively were often paying inflated rates for virtual currency in a system that didn’t protect
them from bad actors. It was the perfect system for the Roblox team… until the government took
notice. Now that people are looking closely at the business model, they don’t like what they see.
The age-verification system isn’t Roblox’s problem. It’s a sign of a much bigger problem,
but it’s one no one can ignore. And as long as people keep looking closely at
how Roblox does business, it’s hard to see the current stock slide reversing itself.
